subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which sociologist is most closely associated with the development of functionalism and the idea of social solidarity?
questions.explain: Durkheim is regarded as a founder of functionalism, stressing social solidarity and shared values.

questions.q: Which sociologist developed functionalist ideas about how society's institutions meet its needs?
questions.explain: Parsons is a key functionalist who saw institutions as working together to meet society's needs.

questions.q: Functionalists argue that social order is maintained mainly through:
questions.explain: Functionalism is a consensus theory, seeing order as based on agreement over shared norms and values.

questions.q: The 'organic analogy' used by functionalists compares society to:
questions.explain: Functionalists compare society to a body, where each institution (organ) performs a function to keep the whole healthy.

questions.q: A school teaches all pupils the same rules, values and a sense of belonging. A functionalist would say the school is performing the function of:
questions.explain: Functionalists see education as socialising pupils into shared values, building solidarity and consensus.

questions.q: Which sociologist founded Marxism?
questions.explain: Marxism takes its name from Karl Marx, who analysed society in terms of class conflict.

questions.q: In Marxist theory, what are the two main social classes?
questions.explain: Marx divided capitalist society into the ruling bourgeoisie and the working-class proletariat.

questions.q: Marxism is best described as which type of theory?
options: A conflict theory based on class inequality
A consensus theory based on shared values
A micro theory of everyday interaction
questions.explain: Marxism is a conflict theory, viewing society as based on unequal, competing class interests.

questions.q: What do Marxists mean by 'false consciousness'?
options: When the working class fail to recognise their own exploitation
When people follow shared moral values
When women accept traditional gender roles
questions.explain: False consciousness is when the proletariat do not see how capitalism exploits them, accepting ruling-class ideology.

questions.q: A factory owner keeps the profits while workers receive low wages for producing goods. A Marxist would describe this as:
questions.explain: Marxists see profit as coming from the exploitation of workers by the owners of the means of production.

questions.q: The term 'patriarchy', used by feminists, refers to:
options: A society organised around male power and dominance
A society based on shared moral values
An economy owned by the ruling class
questions.explain: Patriarchy describes a system in which men hold power and women are disadvantaged.

questions.q: Which three types of feminism are commonly identified?
questions.explain: The main strands studied are liberal, Marxist and radical feminism, each explaining gender inequality differently.

questions.q: Which sociologist is associated with studying gender-role socialisation, including 'canalisation' and 'manipulation'?
questions.explain: Ann Oakley identified processes such as manipulation and canalisation through which children learn gender roles.

questions.q: Radical feminists argue that the main cause of women's oppression is:
questions.explain: Radical feminists see patriarchy as the primary cause of women's oppression across all of society.

questions.q: In a family a girl is given dolls and encouraged to do housework, while her brother is given footballs and told to be tough. A feminist would see this as:
questions.explain: Feminists argue such socialisation teaches gender roles that maintain male dominance.

questions.q: Which sociologist is most associated with labelling theory?
questions.explain: Howard Becker developed labelling theory, showing how labels attached by others shape behaviour.

questions.q: A 'self-fulfilling prophecy' occurs when:
options: A label leads a person to act in line with that label
Society reaches a shared value consensus
Institutions meet the needs of society
questions.explain: A self-fulfilling prophecy happens when a person internalises a label and behaves so it comes true.

questions.q: Interactionism is best described as:
options: A micro approach focusing on small-scale interactions and meanings
A structural theory of class conflict
A consensus theory of shared values
questions.explain: Interactionism is a micro-level approach concerned with how individuals interact and interpret meanings.

questions.q: Which sociologist is associated with the idea that people present themselves to others as if performing on a stage?
questions.explain: Goffman's dramaturgical approach describes how people manage the 'presentation of self' like actors on a stage.

questions.q: A teacher labels a pupil a 'troublemaker'; the pupil then lives up to the label and misbehaves more. An interactionist would call this:
questions.explain: The pupil internalises the negative label and acts it out, making the prophecy come true.
